cards.title: Waterfall pricing from contribution target up to retail price
cards.summary: Work bottom-up from a contribution profit target through CAC, returns/discount allowances, shipping, and COGS to derive the minimum viable retail price for a product.
cards.use_when: Product selection or pricing: deciding whether to launch or keep a SKU, or setting its retail price before comparing to competitors.
steps: Set your contribution profit target first. Work from net profit target plus operating expense share (e.g. 10% net + 10% opex = 20% contribution target). This is the source's illustrative math, not a universal benchmark; use your own P&L.
Add expected CAC for this product based on your ad account and comparable products (source example: $30).
Add a shrink allowance covering returns and discounts (source example: 3% return + 3% discount), expressed as a percentage of price.
Add shipping and fulfillment cost (get a real quote from your courier, source example: $11) and cost of goods (source example: $6).

Combine into a price equation: price must cover COGS + shipping + CAC + shrink allowances and still leave the contribution target. Iterate the price until the contribution margin hits target (source worked example resolved to roughly a $70 price).

Then run competitor research. If the required price is far above the market, decide whether you can credibly position as a premium/blue-ocean alternative. If not, cut the product rather than sell it below the required unit economics.
caveats: Numbers in the source example are illustrative, not benchmarks.
If the math only works at a price nobody will pay and you cannot reposition, the correct answer per the source is not to sell the product.

cards.title: Calculate break-even ROAS and break-even CAC before any discount
cards.summary: Break-even ROAS equals 1 divided by gross margin percentage, and break-even CAC equals gross margin dollars — both must be recalculated during discount periods.
cards.use_when: Pricing, promotions and paid media planning: deciding whether a campaign, ad set or promotion is actually profitable.
steps: Compute gross margin percentage on the item or AOV. With a $100 price and $40 gross margin, margin is 40%.
Break-even ROAS = 1 / gross margin % = 1 / 0.40 = 2.5. Below 2.5 the campaign loses money.
Equivalently, break-even CAC = gross margin dollars ($40). Any CAC above that loses money on first purchase.
Share the break-even number with your internal team and agency so they can flag campaigns running below it.
Recompute the same two numbers for every planned discount, because gross margin dollars fall while COGS, shipping and CAC largely stay fixed.
Recheck before launching a public promotion whether the implied efficiency target is physically achievable on your paid platforms.
caveats: Assumes COGS and shipping are unchanged by the discount, which is the source's simplifying assumption.
Break-even on first purchase only; it ignores repeat purchase profit, so it is a conservative floor for the paid acquisition decision.

cards.title: Model the exponential margin damage of a straight discount
cards.summary: A 30% discount on a 60% COGS item can cut gross margin from 40% to 10%, multiplying the required break-even ROAS by roughly five.
cards.use_when: Promotions and offer design: pressure-testing a discount before running it publicly or on paid acquisition.
steps: Start from the undiscounted economics: $100 price, $60 cost of goods, $40 gross margin, break-even ROAS 2.5 and break-even CAC $40.
Apply the discount to price only: 30% off gives a $70 price while COGS stays $60, leaving $10 gross margin (10%).
Recalculate: break-even ROAS becomes 1 / 0.10 = 10, and break-even CAC becomes $10.

Ask whether that efficiency is achievable. Per the source, a $10 CAC is effectively impossible across paid platforms, meaning this discount cannot be used to acquire new customers — so it should not go out publicly.
If the required uplift is unrealistic (e.g. needing to move from 2x to 12x), rethink the offer structure rather than the discount depth.
caveats: The specific 30%/60% figures are a worked illustration, not a general rule; run the math with your own margin structure.
Discounting is not banned — the source says you must understand how it shifts paid media efficiency targets, and that flat discounts belong on non-moving inventory.

cards.title: Use bundles to give value without eroding gross margin percentage
cards.summary: Bundling raises AOV and typically inflates shipping/fulfillment by far less than the unit count, so you can pass value to the customer while keeping margin percentage intact.
cards.use_when: Offer design and merchandising: when you want a customer-facing deal that does not destroy the unit economics the way a flat discount does.
steps: Identify a product pair or multi-pack where fulfillment cost is roughly fixed per shipment rather than strictly per unit. The source's illustration: moving from one unit to two in the cart inflates shipping cost by about 20%, not 100%.
Model the bundle's gross margin percentage against the single-unit version and confirm it does not degrade.
Use the freed-up margin to fund the perceived discount in the bundle price rather than cutting price on a single unit.
Track the effect on AOV and on allowable CAC — a higher AOV lets you pay more to acquire and still make money.
Position the bundle as a value discrepancy in the market so it functions as the reason to buy rather than as a price cut.
caveats: The ~20% fulfillment inflation figure is a source illustration, not a measured benchmark — verify with your own carrier rates.
Bundle value depends on the items pairing logically and on inventory availability of both SKUs.

cards.title: Design gift-with-purchase offers around the gift's true cost
cards.summary: A low-cost gift with a high perceived retail value can double AOV while giving up only a few dollars of margin.
cards.use_when: Offer design and PDP merchandising: creating a purchase incentive that lifts AOV without compressing gross margin percentage.
steps: Pick the purchase threshold to be a genuine AOV increase (source example: buy two $100 towels to receive the bag).
Choose a gift with a strong perceived value relative to its cost to you — the source's example bag is displayed at $50-$60 on site but costs about $4 in COGS.
Calculate the margin forgone versus the extra revenue captured: giving up $4 of margin to gain an extra $100 in revenue keeps gross margin percentage roughly the same while doubling AOV.
Validate the full unit economics in a spreadsheet before running the offer publicly, baking in your assumptions.
Display the gift's stated value prominently so the perceived value discrepancy does the work of getting the customer over the line.
caveats: The $4 cost and $50-$60 perceived-value figures are a source example; your gift must actually be able to carry that listed price credibly.
Low-cost gifts only work if they are relevant enough to the purchased product to feel like a natural add.

cards.title: Restrict flat discounting to non-moving inventory to convert stock to cash
cards.summary: Straight discounts compress margin badly, so reserve them for slow-moving stock where the alternative is not selling at all.
cards.use_when: Pricing and merchandising: clearing aged inventory or funding a cash conversion push.
steps: Grade your inventory by sell-through — for example A (fast moving), B (medium), C and D (barely moving) — so you know which stock needs intervention.
Apply flat discounts only to stock that is not moving. Per the source, recovering cash at break-even is acceptable because that inventory was not going to sell anyway.
Model the required break-even ROAS/CAC at the discounted price before deciding how deep to go, since discounting raises the efficiency bar steeply.

Where relevant, isolate clearance SKUs from the main catalog and push them through dedicated funnels, landing pages or separate markets so the discount does not erode brand equity in your primary market.
Feed the discounted SKU's economics back into the paid media plan instead of judging it on normal profit KPIs.
caveats: Inventory grade labels and the break-even-is-fine guidance come from the source's framework; confirm your own cash position before accepting zero-margin clearance.
Discounting fast-moving grade A inventory is the mistake this approach is designed to avoid.

cards.title: Compare contribution margin per product, not just CPA
cards.summary: Two SKUs can have very different contribution margins per sale even when a lower-priced one shows the cheaper CPA, which distorts platform bidding.
cards.use_when: Product selection and paid media structure: deciding which SKUs deserve budget and how to segment campaigns.
steps: Build a per-product table with retail price, COGS, gross margin dollars, current CAC/CPA and resulting contribution margin. Source example: a $90 hoodie with $21 COGS, $45 CAC and $24 contribution, versus a t-shirt with $27 gross margin, $15 CAC and $12 contribution.
Compare contribution margin per sale, not efficiency ratios alone. In the example the hoodie delivers about 2x the contribution of the t-shirt.

Recognize that platforms bidding on maximize conversions optimize to lowest CPA, so they will pour spend into the lower-CPA t-shirt even though it produces less profit. Switching to maximize conversion value does not fix it in the source example, because the t-shirt also has the better ROAS.
Segment campaigns by product category aligned to product-level economics so budget is not allocated purely by platform-optimized CPA.

Ask whether high-efficiency SKUs would sell anyway without paid support. If the source's t-shirt sells on its own, removing paid spend lifts its contribution to $27 and frees budget for SKUs that need advertising to achieve sell-through.
caveats: The numerical example is illustrative; rebuild it with your own COGS, CAC and margin data.
Segmenting by product category adds campaign management overhead and may slow learning in the ad account.

cards.title: Measure on a pyramid: platform metrics, finance-grade KPIs, incrementality
cards.summary: Reliability of measurement increases as you move from platform-attributed metrics up to finance-grade KPIs and incrementality tests, while speed of feedback decreases.
cards.use_when: Measurement and reporting: choosing which numbers to trust for budget decisions and how to present them to founders or a leadership team.
steps: Bottom layer: platform metrics such as ROAS, CPA, CTR and multi-touch attribution. Use these only for directional feedback inside a single platform — comparing two Meta campaigns against each other is reasonable.

Avoid comparing ROAS across platforms such as Google versus Meta, because attribution models, funnel position and incremental impact differ. A platform with weak attributed ROAS can still be driving incremental revenue.

Middle layer: finance-grade KPIs such as acquisition MER, CAC and profit contribution, computed from actual new customer counts, actual revenue and actual ad spend rather than platform attribution. Expect these to move more slowly and require longer evaluation windows.
Top layer: incrementality testing using geographic holdouts and control-versus-treatment groups over a defined window (e.g. geo holdouts for 30 days, then compare new customer revenue lift).

Only attempt incrementality testing with real data science capability and proper test design; a spreadsheet-driven holdout will typically produce false 'not incremental' results, overspend or under-deliver.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that the top layer is likely not appropriate for most businesses and is complex to design.
Lower-layer metrics remain necessary for fast, directional campaign and creative feedback even though they are unreliable for cross-channel allocation.

cards.title: Use new-customer MER instead of blended MER
cards.summary: Blended MER lets marketing take credit for returning-customer revenue that would have come back anyway, so delineate new-customer revenue over ad spend.
cards.use_when: Measurement and acquisition budgeting: indexing paid media performance over time and setting acquisition targets.
steps: Compute MER as revenue divided by ad spend (the source notes some teams invert this to a percentage). $100 revenue on $50 ad spend gives a 2x MER.
Strip out returning-customer revenue before drawing conclusions about acquisition, because returning customers would return without advertising.

Calculate new-customer MER as new customer revenue divided by ad spend. In the source's illustration the same business looks like 2x blended but roughly 1.4x on new customers, which may not be profitable.
Present both numbers internally so leadership understands which part of revenue advertising is actually responsible for generating.
Reassess acquisition strategy using the new-customer figure rather than the blended headline.
caveats: Requires reliable separation of new versus returning customer revenue in your analytics/Shopify data.
The 2x and 1.4x figures are illustrations of the arithmetic, not performance benchmarks.

cards.title: Track LTGP to CAC on fixed time windows, not lifetime-forever
cards.summary: Divide gross profit from a customer over a defined window by the cost to acquire them, and interpret the ratio against staged bands rather than treating any result as good.
cards.use_when: Retention and acquisition planning: judging whether paid acquisition is reasonably efficient and how aggressively you can scale spend.
steps: Use lifetime gross profit (LTGP) rather than revenue-based LTV. Many tools report LTV as revenue; in ecommerce you want gross profit.

Fix the time window — the source uses 30-day and 90-day LTGP:CAC, sometimes 365-day for aggressive acquisition. Unbounded LTV keeps rising with the horizon and leads to overspending before cash is realized.
Compute the ratio. Source example: $100 gross profit per customer and $33 CAC gives 3.33.

Apply the source's heuristics: below 1 means you lose money on acquisition and, per the source, most brands in this position do not have retention strong enough to justify it; 1 to 2 is generally not a good position for most brands with only adequate retention (the source says some CPG brands with strong retention can operate here); 2 to 3 is the optimal scaling zone; above 3 is also a mistake because you are under-leveraging paid media.

Translate the target band into a CAC constraint: with $100 gross profit on first order, a 2x ratio means a $50 CAC. Divide your first-order gross profit by two to find the CAC needed to reach the bottom of the optimal band.

If you are below 1, check both sides: acquisition efficiency and whether first-order gross profit is simply too thin (the source suggests under roughly $70 gross profit on first order is likely a problem area) to support paid acquisition at scale.
caveats: The sub-1 / 1-2 / 2-3 / 3+ bands are the source's heuristics, not formulas. The source also states that most brands it audits which lose on acquisition do not have retention strong enough to support it, and that only a very small fraction can deliberately buy customers at a loss.
A CAC payback framing from the source's agency comparison (3-6 months to become profitable on a client) is an illustration of the principle, not an ecommerce benchmark.

cards.title: Analyze new-customer versus returning-customer profit contribution separately
cards.summary: Most ecommerce profit often comes from returning customers because they cost little to re-acquire, while new customer revenue carries the ad spend.
cards.use_when: Retention planning and acquisition budgeting: deciding how hard to push new customer acquisition and how much to invest in retention channels.
steps: Split monthly revenue into new customer revenue and returning customer revenue (source example: $200k total, $140k new, $60k returning).

Apply ad spend against new customer revenue only, then subtract cost of delivery and gross margin to get new-customer profit contribution ($140k - $50k = $90k; at 50% gross margin, $70k - $50k = $20k profit contribution).
Do the same for returning customer revenue, deducting the tools and agency costs that drive repeat revenue (source example: $30k gross profit minus $27.5k costs).
Expect that returning customers may contribute more monthly profit than new customers at this stage; the source describes this as typical.
Use that profit contribution to decide how aggressively you can subsidize acquisition, since returning customer profit can fund higher new-customer CAC.
caveats: Requires clean new versus returning revenue segmentation and allocation of channel/tool costs to the returning side.
The numeric example is illustrative and structured to demonstrate the principle, not a benchmark split.

cards.title: Configure Meta reporting to reduce over-attribution
cards.summary: Exclude view-through conversions and existing customers from reporting to get numbers closer to finance-grade acquisition metrics.
cards.use_when: Paid media measurement and budget decisions: auditing Meta reporting settings and frequency before scaling spend.
steps: Set reporting and optimization to 7-day click rather than view-through windows. The source notes 7-day click ROAS tends to correlate closely with acquisition MER because it excludes view-through conversions that the platform can claim when a user sees an ad but never clicks.
Exclude existing customers from acquisition reporting. They are typically not incremental, and the platform has an incentive to spend against them.
Open breakdown by audience segment to see where spend is actually going, and pull the frequency column.
Per the source, if 7-day frequency is above 8, you are likely overspending on existing customers who are being served more than eight times without incremental effect.
Recognize that platforms benefit from longer attribution windows and broader claiming, so treat their default reporting as promotional rather than conservative.
Verify current interface locations and setting names in the platform before acting, since ad platform reporting options change.
caveats: The frequency cap of 8 over 7 days is the source's heuristic, not a platform default.
7-day click is closer to finance-grade metrics but still relies on platform attribution, so it remains a directional tool.

cards.title: Budgetting existing-customer ad spend from audience size and frequency
cards.summary: Calculate existing-customer ad spend from how many customers you have, your desired frequency, and CPM — not as a percentage of budget.
cards.use_when: Retention advertising and budget allocation: deciding how much to spend retargeting existing customers.
steps: Reject the percentage-of-budget framing. The source argues percentage allocation is the wrong model even for nine-figure brands, because the right spend depends on audience size and desired frequency.
Determine the number of existing customers you want to reach (source example: 300,000 customers).
Choose frequency per month (source example: three exposures).
Find your existing-customer CPM from an audience segment breakdown in the platform.
Multiply: customers x frequency x CPM / 1,000. Source example: 300,000 x 3 x $2.50 CPM gives about $2,250 per month.
Per the source, most brands need to spend far less than they assume here — often a small fraction of what they currently allocate. Verify CPM and interface details in the platform, as these change.
caveats: The $2.50 CPM is explicitly a low illustrative figure; the source notes real CPMs are usually higher, which raises the required spend.
Frequency assumptions should be tested, not treated as optimal — the source suggests a 3 to 6 frequency range as generally sufficient.

cards.title: Solve for the next best dollar across channels
cards.summary: Identify where the next increment of budget produces the most incremental profit by comparing marginal returns across channels, including by pulling budget out of one channel.
cards.use_when: Budget allocation and scaling decisions: deciding where to add or remove the next $10,000 of media spend.
steps: List your primary channels and current spend allocation (source example: Meta $100k, TikTok $70k, Google $50k).

For each channel, answer: if we added an extra $10,000 here, what incremental revenue would it return? Derive this from controlled incrementality tests or, at lower revenue, marketing mix models and experienced intuition.

Run the inverse test as well: if you pulled $10,000 out of one channel and moved it to another, would ROI improve? The source example compares a 2x return on the removed spend against a 4x return on new customer revenue elsewhere.
Keep scaling the most efficient channel until its marginal return falls to the level available elsewhere.
Spend up to the point where incremental acquisition MER hits break-even. Per the source, that is where you stop increasing spend in that channel.
Only after you have reached that profit frontier across your primary channels should you consider adding tertiary channels.
caveats: Reliable marginal returns require incrementality testing, which the source says needs real data science capability; for seven-figure brands the source says the allocation question is often answerable intuitively by a strong performance marketer.
Per the source, avoid spreading spend across many tertiary channels before maximizing the primary ones.

cards.title: Read ROAS as correlation, not causation
cards.summary: ROAS relies on attribution, which links correlated events rather than proving the ad caused the purchase, so it over-credits bottom-funnel channels.
cards.use_when: Measurement, channel review and executive reporting: defending or cutting a channel when ROAS numbers look weak.
steps: Treat platform attribution as correlation. A clicked ad followed by a purchase does not prove the ad caused the purchase, just as rising ice cream sales and swimming deaths correlate with summer rather than causing each other.
Expect over-attribution to bottom-of-funnel: a billboard and TV ad may create awareness while the Facebook click that precedes the purchase takes all the credit.

Watch for the cross-channel pattern: spend in a top-of-funnel channel can lift attributed ROAS in the mid and lower funnel channels while its own ROAS stays weak. Cutting the top-of-funnel channel on its ROAS alone risks starving the bottom of the funnel.
Do not let a leadership team reallocate budget purely from per-channel ROAS dashboards — the source describes this as a fundamentally bad decision.
Use ROAS for directional, within-platform campaign and creative feedback, and move business-level questions to finance-grade metrics and incrementality testing.
caveats: The specific platform ordering described by the source (e.g. one channel under-attributing while another captures the demand) is described as a current, non-universal circumstance that may change.
Attribution remains useful for fast, directional decisions inside a single platform.

cards.title: Design geographic holdout incrementality tests for media decisions
cards.summary: Split geographies into control and treatment, change spend in one group, and measure the difference in new customer revenue to estimate true incremental impact.
cards.use_when: Measurement: validating whether a channel, campaign or budget change actually drives incremental revenue, especially for larger businesses.
steps: Select a geography that can be held out — the source uses states in the US and notes that Australia may require commuting-zone splits because there are not enough states.

Choose treatment and control areas: hold out an area (the source sometimes uses two adjacent states) and increase spend everywhere else, or increase spend in the treatment only, or cut spend entirely — the design depends on the question.
Run the test over a defined window, such as 30 days, and compare new customer revenue realization between control and treatment.
Compute the incremental ROAS from the lift in new customer revenue attributable to the spend change.
Use the result to inform budget allocation rather than relying on platform-attributed ROAS alone.
caveats: The source explicitly warns against replicating this from a spreadsheet. Poorly designed tests will almost always show 'states aren't incremental', cause overspending or underspending, and fail to produce statistically relevant results. This requires at least a fundamental understanding of data science.
Incrementality testing is slow and you cannot run many of them, which limits its use for day-to-day campaign decisions.
This is described as most critical for businesses above roughly $10 million a month with multi-market or omni-channel presence; it is described as probably not applicable to about 80% of viewers.

cards.title: Account for cash conversion cycle before promising rapid scaling
cards.summary: The binding constraint on ecommerce growth is often the cash conversion cycle — DIIO plus DSO minus DPO — not ad efficiency or media budget.
cards.use_when: Growth planning and replenishment: setting realistic scale targets and coordinating marketing spend with inventory cash requirements.
steps: Understand the formula: cash conversion cycle equals days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payable outstanding.

Trace how gross profit from current sales funds the next purchase order. The source's illustration: $50 gross profit per 10 units only funds roughly 11 units next time, so the business grows slowly regardless of ad efficiency.
Add supplier lead time and payment terms. With a 90-day lead time and full upfront payment, you may go out of stock for the full 90 days between selling through and receiving the next order.

Evaluate the three levers: negotiate better supplier terms (e.g. pay 20% upfront and the rest on shipping, potentially cutting the out-of-stock gap to the shipping time of about 20 days), shorten manufacturing lead time (e.g. from 90 to 30 days), or use inventory financing.
Be cautious with financing: it is expensive, usually requires collateral, and requires future units to sell at sufficient efficiency to repay the loan.
Before agreeing to aggressive spend increases, check whether the working capital exists to buy the inventory that scale will require.
caveats: The 90/30-day lead times, 20% upfront and 20-day shipping figures are source illustrations, not typical values.

The source describes cases where a business grew from $2 million to $7 million a year with agency-driven spend scaling while net margins compressed toward zero because growth was funded by debt — presented as a risk pattern, not a prediction.

cards.title: Read the balance sheet alongside the P&L to see real ecommerce profit
cards.summary: Reported profit is not cash, because ecommerce profit is typically reinvested into future inventory, which sits on the balance sheet.
cards.use_when: Founder-level reporting and growth decisions: interpreting profit figures and communicating the true cash position.
steps: Treat the P&L and balance sheet as separate signals. A brand showing $2 million annual profit may have $3 million of unsold inventory on the balance sheet.
Recognize that for most ecommerce businesses the balance sheet assets are primarily unsold inventory plus cash — not buildings or equipment — unless the business owns offices or warehouses.
If profit for the period is $2 million but $3 million in inventory did not sell, the business is down about $1 million in cash despite the reported profit.
When posting profit figures, account for the cash committed to future inventory purchasing before treating profit as available to founders.
Use this framing when deciding whether to fund higher acquisition spend or larger inventory buys.
caveats: The $2 million profit and $3 million inventory figures are source illustrations to demonstrate the mechanism.

The source notes this reinvestment dynamic makes ecommerce paid media materially more complex than service or SaaS businesses; a specific agency CAC payback example (3-6 months) is used as a comparison, not an ecommerce benchmark.

cards.title: Grade inventory and rationalize SKUs to avoid the inventory death spiral
cards.summary: Product launches that fail land as slow-moving stock, adding cash to the balance sheet and constraining growth unless you rationalize SKU count and proactively clear graded stock.
cards.use_when: Product selection, inventory management and merchandise planning: deciding which SKUs to keep, launch or clear, and how to brief the paid media team.
steps: Grade inventory by sell-through: grade A fast moving, grade B medium, grade C and D slow or not moving. The source notes Shopify auto-ranks inventory in the products area, so verify current interface behavior yourself.
Recognize the launch pattern: new products often land 30-40% of inventory through organic and existing customer demand, then stall into grade C or D.
When a SKU stalls, measure days of inventory on hand (source example: 400 days) to quantify how long the cash will be tied up.
Rationalize SKU count down as new products are introduced, rather than letting slow sellers accumulate on the balance sheet.

Coordinate marketing and finance so the paid media team knows which grades need to be pushed. This is presented as a common failure: agencies and paid teams KPI'd only on profit will never prioritize grade B/C/D inventory, yet clearing that inventory is how it converts back to cash.

When rationalizing, convert stalled stock back to cash via paid media at break-even or slight loss, isolated funnels/offer pages, or by launching it into a new market where heavy discounting will not erode brand equity in the primary market.
caveats: The source warns against treating product-led growth as universally applicable: single-product brands at scale are concentrated in the supplements space (Grunes, AG1, IM8 are cited), where a product can be repositioned into a large addressable market. Most ecommerce brands are advised to plan future product launches instead.
The 400-day inventory figure and the 30-40% initial sell-through are source illustrations.
